## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, so the first round spreads its bets. The default budget is only 32 PPO updates of 4,096 steps, on a stream of fresh designs. That makes sample count and data diversity likely bottlenecks, so the recipe is worth testing on its own. On the architecture side, each placement is right only if the cells at the brick's landing layer (the maximum height under its footprint) are missing target cells and nothing below them is still missing. That is a level-indexed AND under a max over the footprint. The baseline's small max/min/avg head can represent this, but only with little spare capacity. The three candidates are: (1) the recipe alone, with fewer PPO epochs and so more fresh samples; (2) shifting compute from the trunk into a larger footprint head that also sees the stem's per-column features directly; (3) a new head that learns a soft landing-level distribution and uses it to select per-level footprint features.

### Round 2
Scores are hidden, so only these facts are known: all three round-1 trials trained without errors, and the baseline costs about 3.2M MACs per sample. The task gives two leads. First, every episode uses a fresh random design, so seeing more samples per FLOP (fewer PPO epochs) is likely to help. Second, the placement head only sees a 5x5 trunk receptive field and gets no global context. Global context matters for order: for example, whether the cells under a planned overhang must be filled before the overhang brick goes on, and when to call DONE. This round makes three changes: (1) push the sample-efficiency direction further with 1 PPO epoch; (2) add r1c1's 2-epoch recipe plus a cheap global vector broadcast into the placement head; (3) add r1c1's 2-epoch recipe plus one light self-attention layer over all cells, so placement features see the whole grid.

### Round 3
All six trials trained without errors, but the scores are hidden, so I can't rank them or tell what helped. Because scores are hidden, separating the effect of each change gains nothing. Only the final selection, which uses the real dev scores, matters. So this round aims to make it likely that at least one trial is strong, by stacking plausible gains. One thing all trials so far share is gamma 0.95 with GAE lambda 0.9. The +1 exact-build bonus comes at the end of an episode of 6 to 33 placements, so at 0.95 the early placements barely see it (0.95^16 ≈ 0.44). Choosing when to stop and avoiding wrong cells that can never be removed both depend on long-horizon credit. So all three candidates use gamma 0.99 with lambda 0.95. Two of them stack this on architecture changes: the global broadcast plus cell attention, and a deeper residual trunk.

### Round 4
I can't see any scores, so these choices rest on priors, not evidence. Every trial so far trained without errors, including 1 epoch at 405k steps (r2c1), so time limits aren't a risk at these sizes. My priors: (1) with a fresh design every episode and a dense reward, more samples per FLOP (fewer PPO epochs) probably helps; (2) gamma 0.99 should carry the +1 exact-build bonus back to early placements; (3) the global broadcast costs almost nothing and gives each placement score the overall build state; (4) attention or depth could help with ordering, at a cost in samples. This is the last round, so I'm aiming for the strongest combinations rather than clean single-variable tests. All three candidates use 1 PPO epoch with gamma 0.99 and lambda 0.95. They differ only in the network's context range: local (the base network plus the broadcast), global attention, or a deeper conv trunk with a stem skip.
